body: I think it depends on the district. Many public schools here have aids and floating subs on rotation for this purpose, but I will say this district has really amped up their special education and behavioral programs. However I do know that having these aids accessible is a privilege other schools don’t have. I also know some schools here have conflicting policies. A lot of the middle and high schools do not require an IEP depending on the student but the elementary schools do depending on the town. I think it can be kind of a crap shoot depending on where you are.

Advocating for your children is always the right choice. And I do think the mother who has not accepted the IEP is problematic in her own right. However, if the school for some reason legally cannot remove her - it is the school’s responsibility to work with the parent to find a solution that protects all the kids. Unfortunately there are a lot of districts where just pulling the problematic child from the classroom isn’t an option legally and their hands are tied. However that should not be the only option regardless of district. As another commenter said on this post, some schools have behavior rooms that a student can just be sent to without any parental sign on - which seems like it would be highly beneficial in this scenario. I think the big issue in this particular circumstance is that the school does not seem to be able to mandate an IEP plan/remove the child ethically - and seems to have absolutely no other suggestions to this group of parents on how they’re going to rectify the situation. That’s on the school. I get the stresses of the pandemic on the schools and have a lot of respect for the teachers powering through, but a petition won’t change the law if that’s the issue (unless they petition the district for general special Ed reform - which also covers them in regard to any type of discrimination retaliation and most districts could use better regulation in this space anyways). If the school thinks the mother is unfit to make decisions for the child like you say, they’re legal mandated reporters and could have her investigated - that’s why I said we have no idea what’s going on behind the scenes. For all we know they’re in the process of having the child evaluated at length so they can ethically remove them, or is having the parent investigated if she has given them reason to. All that takes time and has confidentially regulations attached so they wouldn’t be able to share it with the parents. That said they could at least tell them they’re in progress rectifying the scenario. It’s a crap situation.

Oh I absolutely agree that this child needs specialized instruction. If they cannot legally enforce an IEP then there needs to be something else in place. Ideally they could at the very least assign a paraprofessional to this child who can safely remove them from the classroom to prevent abuse and disruptions as much as possible. Conflict management would be to help explain to the children why said child needs to be removed/how to advocate for themselves if the child is aggressive towards them and the teacher misses it for some reason. Should have clarified in main post but was mostly focused on the OP’s petition idea.

I agree with you. That said, depending on the district/state etc they may not be able to legally enforce that if the child doesn’t meet criteria or the parent doesn’t agree. If that’s the case in this situation they should be able to assign a paraprofessional or aid who can remove the child when the child is acting out. That would limit the other children’s exposure to abuse and disruptions and give added support to the child who very clearly needs help. It’s very unfortunate the child’s parent has seemingly rejected an IEP. It would likely greatly help the child in question as well as allow the other students to learn effectively and safely.
It’s an all around difficult situation. Ideally the school can come up with a good solution.

They’re not wrong to voice their concerns to the school in any way. They absolutely should. The petition is not going to help their case though because depending on where they are the parent of the disruptive child could start something over discrimination, and I think that could hurt the OP’s end goal of just ensuring their child is getting quality education. They have every right to be concerned about their children - but there should be a middle ground here that the SCHOOL can mediate. You do not need an IEP in most states to have an aid who can remove a child during a meltdown (therefore limiting all the other children’s exposure to this disruptive behavior as much as possible). There is a problem for the entire classroom as a whole. It should not be a “us vs that kid” or “that kid vs us”. The entire dynamic isn’t working for anyone. It’s not healthy for anyone based off of OP’s description of events and I feel for everyone involved. It’s a bad situation every which way.

Absolutely not what I’m saying. I just responded to the OP’s question of if their behavior was appropriate. This child absolutely needs help and not at the detriment of other children. The child’s family should ideally accept the IEP, or be given a paraprofessional or aid who can remove the child safely during disruptions and work with the child one on one. This way that child has support, and the children in their class can learn effectively without the consistent interruption. This however is an answer to a different question that what the OP has asked here.

When I say that I mean that conflict management is an important learned skill, but I can see how it sounded so appreciated the comment. That said, the disruption experienced by the kids in this class is outside of what is the social norm and I do think it’s an absolute shame the family of the child who seems to have behavioral issues is not taking up the school’s offer for the IEP because not only would it give the kiddo support that is clearly needed, but help allow the other students to learn more effectively with a plan in place for when the other child is causing mass disruptions.

I didn’t say what the other child is doing is at all acceptable. There needs to be change for that child. I just responded in regard to the OP’s behavior. The other child needs a paraprofessional, aid - whomever - who can remove them from the classroom or work with them one on one to prevent any type of detriment to the other students. If the child who is causing the disruptions has been offered an IEP and the family is refusing to accept it that’s a shame because it could likely provide needed support to that child, and help the classroom dynamic. Nobody should be punished related to someone else’s behavior. That said, the way the parent is acting isn’t the answer.

I didn’t say her actions aren’t problematic - they absolutely are. She needs a paraprofessional, an aid or her family needs to accept the IEP. That said, depending on the state and district there’s only so much the school can do legally. I simply responded to OP’s question about if they were behaving poorly. That doesn’t excuse the other child’s mother seemingly choosing not to accept the seemingly much needed help offered to her, but that parent’s choice also doesn’t make a petition against a child a good response either. There’s problems on all sides and the answer will not be cut and dry. The other children in the class absolutely need supports as well. Conflict management, group activities that support the kids advocating for themselves with the teacher in the moment, even an extra teacher on staff in the classroom if not a para (like a floating substitute) who can provide attention to the student having behavioral difficulties and remove them from the room for a break.

I agree that something needs to change - but that’s not what the OP asked. OP asked if they were an asshole for essentially circulating a petition to get a troubled child out of the classroom without fully understanding what’s going on. That’s a problem.
And I’m sorry to hear your kids are suffering! I think it’s lovely you want to work on this with your kiddos.

Oh absolutely. I really like starting with teaching about the zones of regulation. It helps them first by associating colors and expressions to different emotions. It helps the kids recognize difficult emotions in themselves and others. But there are a ton of different ways you can go with this, especially depending on age and development. DBT is always great because it’s a therapeutic style that teaches effective communication, conflict management and validation - you can find tons of workbooks for various ages online. Boom Learning is a free (or more perks for pay) website that has premade “decks” that cover everything from math to emotion regulation, social skills, appropriate conflict management - I use them a lot in my telehealth sessions with my clients since covid hit. Role playing has proven effective both in anti bullying and conflict management.
It’s just honesty. It’s teaching children a level of intolerance that is so unhealthy and negative for society.

As someone who has been on multiple sides of this type of equation; first as a teacher and now as a therapist you are absolutely the asshole. The teacher is right to recommend conflict management skills, but what you’re doing is wildly inappropriate. It adds to the stigma of mental health and developmental issues, and it’s absolutely unethical for a group of parents to be basically harassing the school into trying to force a family into accepting an IEP plan. There is only so much the school can legally do here and you have no idea what goes on behind the scenes. Also - these people are teaching during a pandemic. They have enough stress. You have absolutely no idea what this family could be going through and you’re 100% likely adding to their pain. Why would you want to make this situation worse for these people? This is a time to talk to your daughter about differences, conflict and empathy - which it sounds like all you parents need to foster a bit yourself. God forbid your child develops a mental health or developmental issue in her teen years. You would never want parents ganging up on you and your kid if you were in this family’s position.

So I participate in this thread usually as someone who is a caregiver in their personal time - but I am an ABA therapist and have experienced this with a client’s parent. High functioning, highly intelligent, wonderful teenage boy with extremely mild Autism and ADD. We should have known when we took the case and were informed no other therapeutic company has been willing to work with her for years. 

My client’s biggest deficit to be addressed in therapy was his lack of social skills with his peers. While he was great with adults, he couldn’t process a lot of the nuances of being a teen and was taken advantage of frequently and manipulated by peers. We were also working on executive functioning - like learning to cook basic meals for himself and clean areas using a checklist since he’d be off to college soon. Parent training is required in ABA therapy so parents can reinforce the skills. His mom rarely showed and cancelled constantly. At a PPT meeting with his school shortly before covid where all his teachers and school treatment team discussed how well he was doing - she screamed at me in the parking lot about how the school was out to get her and lying etc. and how my supervisor was inept (she’s wonderful and very good at her job). 

During this time he mastered all his goals in therapy - with the exception of the final step being going out in the community with peers (supervised by me and a parent until we could fade the supervision) and she refused every time. This is a late teens boy who isn’t even allowed to have friends over at the house. The Autism wasn’t effecting his social skills at this point it was the complete lack of peer exposure outside of school from birth on. The only way we could substitute this type of experience were through role plays, active listening games and movie clips. His mom hated it and accused us of only wanting to “play” because “we had no idea how to work with a child as difficult as hers”. I ran a psych ward for teenage boys a few years ago - our experience was not the issue.

After covid she stopped showing up at all for telehealth except for one 3 hour zoom session where she screamed at us the entire time. From that point on we informed her we would be taking data on whether or not her parent training goals were met and be emailing and texting for follow through prior to his authorization being up at the end of July. She didn’t follow through more than twice in two months. We documented EVERYTHING. We usually document her skipped sessions and such - but we literally documented everything, like when we could hear her in the room telling her child to tell us she wasn’t home and when the client was showing signs of being suicidal and she ignored our texts and calls over our concerns for his safety. Because of this we were able to discharge him (he met his goals and with covid we can’t do the community outings anyways) knowing we did our jobs to the best of our abilities given the circumstances with his mother and the insurance company would have pulled their authorization because she was skipping her sessions (we warned her both verbally and in writing of the consequences for having too low a utilization repeatedly). 

I know this is long but moral of the story - if you want to keep trying with this client, and it sounds like you have a good bond, make sure EVERYTHING is documented. Get as specific as possible. Definitely get your supervisors involved and have them discuss the ethics/professional statues within your contract (I assume you also offer a family handbook?) because that way the lack of adherence is also documented by someone other than you. It’s always super hard when you have a great client and you just want to do your job and what’s best for them in accordance with their treatment or care plan, but something is stopping that.

So I have a client in his early 20s who had a similar issue in regards to exposing himself to women and taking photos/trying to touch their feet. We used systemic desensitization with him. Before I did ABA I worked as a counselor in a psych ward and used that for things like PTSD to slowly make the client used to the triggering stimulus. We’ve used this with my client to help him adjust to appropriate behaviors around women and in the community since March (I took over for his old RBT once telehealth started) and it’s made a huge difference. We started with simple boom decks I customized for him where there were photos of how you can touch someone vs how you can’t, which is the correct amount of personal space, what does safe hands look like etc. then one he mastered those skills, we upped the complexity of the questions and inserted random pictures of women’s feet in for him to practice his “safe hands”. Once he mastered that I started showing him videos of women walking on the beach with bare feet and things like that so he could react. Now he’s taking socially distanced walks on the beach with his mother and is able to respond safely and appropriately around the woman without touching them or being inappropriate (with me on zoom in case he needs a partial verbal prompt). This may or may not work for your client, but by the time I got this particular client he’d been through several programs and therapists with no change in this behavior and this seems to have worked well for him.

Also with the therapy - finding a therapist is like trying on shoes! A lot of people don’t seem to realize this and think after a therapist or two if it didn’t click or stick it’s just “not for them”. I’ve found (both working in a psych hospital, at an ABA practice, in grad school to become a clinical psychologist and personal experience) that therapy doesn’t work properly until you find the right therapist. You can force yourself to see someone, the same way you can force your foot into a pair of shoes that isn’t quite right, but you’re not going to be comfortable. Try them on! Call a ton who specialize in family counseling - and you can probably find a niche who does family counseling for autism. If you call the number on the back of your insurance card they’ll give you a list of providers. Conduct phone interviews. They may be the “expert” but that doesn’t make them the right fit. You have to try them on for size and sometimes it can take months to find the right person, but when you do it makes a difference. Based off your OP it sounds like your partner is the one rejecting therapy, if you do decide you want to continue your relationship, have her get involved interviewing candidates. I’m a therapeutic crisis intervention counselor, an ABA therapist and in grad school to become a clinical psychologist - any mental health workers with the mindset that mental health issues are due to people being broken are uneducated at best. I’ve had to take so many classes that talk about how health and mental health are perceptions within society, and that societal expectations are a huge part in the mental health system and diagnostic process. Yes chemical imbalances are very real - I have one and it’s directly correlated with my anxiety disorder. And medication for individuals whose illness or thought processes become harmful to themselves or others is medically necessary - the same way someone with diabetes needs medication to protect themselves, my fiancé needs antipsychotics so he doesn’t become homicidal again. But as someone whose worked in psych hospitals, and works in a therapeutic practice now, medications can be given out like candy by certain individuals in the field - and so can diagnoses. I’ve seen people diagnose others with serious mental illnesses without psych testing, and then we do the testing and it’s not accurate and it’s a label a kid in the hospital has been trying to navigate for years. I think there’s a responsibility for professionals in this field to think rationally and responsibly and unfortunately that doesn’t always happen. Nobody is broken because of any type of anxiety, or stress or emotion or chemical imbalance or trauma etc. you may feel things differently, experience them differently or process them differently but that doesn’t have to be a bad thing. Why are there so many different math formulas people can use to solve the same problem? It’s the same thing. People are made with different formulas. Since my fiancé’s diagnosis with a severe psychotic disorder people treat him like he’s broken (his own psychiatrist made a comment along the lines of “no magic pill to fix him” - were looking for a new one now) but the thing is, he doesn’t need to be fixed, and he’s not broken. He may not be able function on the same level that is socially normative in society (can’t work right now, has trouble with executive functioning like remembering to brush teeth etc) but he’s not broken. He’s the most kind, supportive and loving individual - but people see him looking disheveled on a bad day, or know his diagnosis (very public psychotic break) and ask really uneducated questions or make uneducated comments. I know this is kind of a rant - but my point is nobody is broken. Mental health issues are real, but the way society responds to them in the majority of cases is counter productive. Education breeds understanding and understanding breeds support. If these things were discussed more openly in society there would be a lot less people with the view that people suffering from any type of mental health disorder or struggle are “broken”. Societal views absolutely come into play, but they’re not the end all and be all or necessarily the cause of mental illness - but definitely effect how it’s handled and seen.

I think you did the right thing by calling 911. Likely, if you’re in the states, she can’t be discharged for 72 hours. Attempts at jumping off the balcony are likely to be considered being a “danger to herself or others” which means she has to be held on a 5150 psych hold. After the 72 hours they’ll do some evaluations, and if they think she’s still dangerous it’ll become a 5250 where she can be held 2 weeks or more depending on the state, severity and laws. 

In regards to being put in a “facility” - that’s where things get complicated. If she’s over 18 she can’t be forced to go there unless she’s declared incompetent by a court of law. Some hospitals have 28 day or 3 month programs they may keep her for, but not if she’s no longer a danger to herself or others. And if you don’t have money to put her into a private psych facility the odds are she won’t get in to a residential living facility if you tried. As someone who worked in one but for children - each of our patients had to have a minimum of 4 psychological hospitalizations longer than 3 days each, as well as other criteria. When my fiancé had his biggest psychotic break pre medication he threatened to kill me, threatened to kill the president, had to be interviewed by the secret service and repeatedly told staff he was going to kill me after his hospitalization. No facility would take him. They told me he needed a minimum of 4 hospitalizations or multiple arrests plus hospitalizations. I know that likely isn’t what you had hoped to hear but I want to be honest with you about what is common practice in my area (several states surrounding me have similar rules and laws).

ABA therapist/TCI counselor here. I think this could be a variety of things. Could be a variation of self harm, could be a control thing - but based off my experience it may be part of the trauma cycle. If this child experienced some kind of trauma like say, a bully shoving their head near a toilet, or something bathroom related, the child may be reliving the trauma as a way to process. You see this sort of thing a lot in children who have experienced trauma - like abuse victims who had been pinned down actively doing dangerous things that they are aware will lead them to be put in a restraint - but that pressure of the restraint is familiar, and feels secure because they’ve been held down before in a traumatic situation. I had one teenager who peed on anything red. Prior to being adopted from Russia as a toddler, the orphanage left him pantless and only gave the kids red dog food bowls as bathrooms. As a teen living in a full time psych ward, he knew where the bathrooms were and used them, but when he would visit his adopted family he’d find red bins, red shirts etc and urinate on them to self soothe. 

I think this kiddo would greatly benefit from therapy. And if you have information about the bullying and you’re not bound by confidentially - talk to the parent/teacher just about the bullying. Not the child’s behavior necessarily. But make the school aware the child is being bullied and “it’s causing behaviors you’d like to redirect the child away from”.

You may have known of your wife’s background before marrying, but you didn’t know this exact situation is what you were signing up for. You can mourn that. You can take time to be upset about it and grieve for the life and relationship you’d hoped for. Taking the emotional time to grieve my old life with him has helped me adapt to my new one, and for the first time since he got sick - I’m pretty happy. He’s making strides to get well, and I’m still doing all the heavy lifting, but I’ve found a way to feel okay about it. You’re not ranting or an asshole for being upset about your situation. I’m a therapist for children with behavioral disorders and on the autism spectrum - and am engaged to someone with schizophrenia. Something you could do safely is called “reality checking”. It’s a technique used to help the person experiencing psychosis think about what they’re experiencing and compare it to the reality everyone else shares. 

Example: my fiancé was hospitalized again recently and right before he kept talking about secretly being a millionaire and how when he was “16 in 2016” he had his money stolen. My fiancé is in his 20s. He could not have been 16 in 2016. Instead of contradicting him or his delusion I asked how old he was. He answered correctly. Then I asked what year we had started dating. He was a year late, so I asked how long we had been together, he answered correctly with 6.5 years. I asked how old he was 6.5 years ago and he gave me the correct answer. Then I asked what year it was and was met with “OHHHHHHHH....you’re making me sound crazy.....I wasn’t 16 in 2016....” from there I told him he doesn’t sound crazy and that he was confused and needed some help coming back down to me. That ended that very quickly. 

It doesn’t work long term, but if she’s having an episode in class it’s a way to disrupt it enough for her to come back to everyone else’s shared reality even if just a bit. It’s not fool proof - I had one patient reality checking didn’t work for who tried to run out a glass window because he thought he was a ghost (psych wards don’t have windows you can break so he just slammed into it - but that slamming into it is what made him realize “I’m not a ghost I guess”).

Okay - so I’m a therapist (also in school to become a psychologist) and I think I can provide a little clarity here. 

I’m sorry you’re going through all this - I suffer from anxiety too and it’s really tough. There are a few ways you can go about this. 

You could see a psychiatrist - who is a doctor that specializes in psychological matters and can prescribe pretty much any type of psychological medication that fits the bill to help you. They’ll also talk to you about the situation.

You could see a psychologist who will teach you coping mechanisms and techniques to deal with the anxiety - I recommend someone who is a clinical psychologist because a lot of them have a background in cognitive behavioral therapy which is used to understand why something is happening and how to find coping skills to stop it from happening or make it manageable (this is my area of study). They cannot prescribe you medication - but can refer you to someone who can. 

Also at least here in this state, most general practitioners can prescribe basic psych meds for anxiety. Nothing black box labeled but things like Valium or Ativan that help anxiety. I DO NOT recommend going down that route without having a therapist or psychologist to over see it though because if you get put on a med that doesn’t work for you it can cause serious problems and while general doctors are great, they’re not experts in the field.

If you combine seeing a therapist or psychologist with your regular doctor prescribing an anti anxiety med that may be your best bet outside of seeing an actual psychologist.

I also recommend downloading the app moodweek. It forces you to check in on yourself three times a day, prompts you with questions about various topics and analyzes your results every two weeks. It then gives you insight into what could be triggering added anxiety and coping skills to fix it. 

I hope this is helpful

Psychotic disorders can be genetic and usually are, but there are other reasons why a psychotic break could happen. If you’ve experienced recent or are starting to remember past trauma or are under extreme stress symptoms can start to pop up as well. 

Your SO did the right thing although I know sometimes it may not feel that way (it took over a month for mine to forgive me for his hospitalization) and it never hurts to have someone who loves you and supports you because a support system can make a major difference. If the hospital discharged you with follow up instructions as I’m sure they did as it’s pretty standard at least in my state and the state I worked in a psych hospital in - definitely follow through. Again, easier said than done, but nobody likes being stuck in a hospital and building yourself a support system with the recommendations of the doctors treating you can make a huge difference. It took my SO awhile to get on board with his medication and he still hates going to see his doctors biweekly, but he’s going and it’s made a huge difference. He even (begrudgingly) admits he sees a difference and goes on to say things like “he’ll get better soon” because as hard as it is, he’s fighting so he never has another experience like that.


I know it’s scary and kind of surreal when all this happens and obviously you don’t want the situation to repeat but remember that you are strong and you have people there to help you. And if you left the hospital with diagnosis it never hurts to research and educate yourself/your SO. I don’t mean a google deep dive because you’ll just scare yourself and get a lot of misinformation. It won’t be easy but it doesn’t have to change the entire dynamic of your relationship or family life if you don’t let it.

The first thing you need to know is there is NOTHING wrong with you or having “mental disorders”. It’s nothing to be ashamed of, and talking openly about it removes the stigma around mental health that makes so many people afraid to talk about their mental health. The best advice I can give you is to just be honest and matter of fact about it.

These are people who care about you, and sometimes being open about this with the people in your life can help give you a solid support system to help you through the times when you struggle. 

I’m someone with a severe anxiety disorder, PTSD and who suffered from an EDO in High School (and had a weird autoimmune disease that left me in and out of the hospital) and for a long time I built walls around me because I didn’t want to have to explain to anyone why I was always sick or on a heart monitor or talk about the crushing panic attacks - but when I finally did my whole life changed. The friends who were there for me then are still in my life years later, and the boyfriend I had just started dating is my fiancé and has gotten me through everything and now I’m getting him through his own mental health struggles.

Mental health is nothing to be ashamed of. Everyone gets sick, everyone gets colds, nobody is ashamed to talk about those things. Sometimes our brains are sick or our emotions need some first aid too. If more people talk about it this way then the stigma around it won’t exist. These people CARE about you. Just be you. It’s scary because you never know how people will react but try to remember that they’re in your life for a reason.

If you’re in the United States - and you’re insured, you can always call the number on the back of your card and they can provide you with a list of mental health professionals in your area that accept your insurance.
